title: Women and children first
eyebrow: CETI · data · the Titanic’s 2,201 people, pooled and split by class
lede: The rule held on average. Split the same boxes by class and a third-class child lived as often as a first-class man.

chapters.title: The plan: 2,201 boxes, pooled, then split
Deck level: who lived, by class
Which group does the average leave out?

captions: “Women and children first.” The rule everyone remembers.
Did it hold that night for every child aboard?
The Titanic, April 1912. One box is one person aboard.
Passengers and crew: everyone the inquiry counted.
2,201 people. Lit boxes are the ones who lived.
711 lived. 1,490 did not.
Lived: 316 of 425 women, 57 of 109 children, 338 of 1,667 men.
Women and children together: 373 of 534, or 70 %. Men: 20 %.
On average the rule held. Now split the same 2,201 by class.
First, second, third class and the crew. No box added or removed.
Each slab: how many were aboard, and how many lived.
Children in first and second class: 30 of 30 lived.
Children in third class: 27 of 79 lived. 52 did not.
Men in first class: 57 of 175 lived.
34 % and 33 %: a third-class child lived as often as a first-class man.
About 3 in 10 of each. Class weighed as much as being a child.
The crew: 885 people, 40 % of everyone aboard. 212 lived.
Of the 1,667 men, 1,324 were crew or third class. The men’s 20 % is mostly them.
Monday: your “on average” result. Which group does it leave out?
One night, one inquiry’s count: it shows who lived, not why.

brand.takeaway: True on average is not true for every group.
